---
title: "Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data"
---

*Status: available for the two published indicators (mortality rates and
life expectancy). The regional-comparison step awaits sub-provincial
ingestion (milestone M3 in the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md)).*

In this tutorial you will fetch a headline health indicator for British
Columbia, build it from source into a tidy dataset, and look at its
trajectory — using only reproducible, documented steps. No prior
familiarity with the project is assumed.

## Prerequisites

- A working environment (see [How to contribute](../how-to/contribute.qmd)):
  Quarto and `uv` installed, `uv sync` run once.
- No data needs to be present beforehand — we fetch it in step 2.

## 1. See what the project knows about

Lists the indicators the pipeline can build, and the catalogued data
sources behind them:

```bash
uv run sohbc indicators
uv run sohbc list
```

`indicators` lists the entries the pipeline can build — mortality rates,
life expectancy, and a family of survey indicators (life satisfaction,
perceived health and mental health, anxiety and mood disorders, diabetes,
high blood pressure, having a regular provider, daily smoking) — each
tagged with its measurement-framework domain. `list` shows the catalogued
sources; only a few are marked `auto` (the pipeline can fetch them without
a browser).

## 2. Fetch the raw source

Each indicator names a catalogued source. Life expectancy comes from
Statistics Canada's life tables. Fetch it into the reproducible local
layout:

```bash
uv run sohbc fetch statcan_life_tables
```

The raw response lands in `data/raw/statcan_life_tables/` and a checksum
is recorded in `data/manifest.json`. Raw data is **not** committed: the
catalogue and this command are what make it reproducible.

## 3. Build the tidy dataset

Turn the raw table into a published, tidy dataset:

```bash
uv run sohbc build life_expectancy_bc
```

This writes `data/published/life_expectancy_bc.csv` plus trend-test JSON.
Look at the first rows:

```bash
head -4 data/published/life_expectancy_bc.csv
```

Every datum carries its reference date, geography, age group, sex, and
characteristic, so nothing about its resolution is lost (a project rule —
see the [measurement framework](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd)).

## 4. Look at the trajectory

Load the tidy file and plot the series in the language of your choice. The
R-and-Python-agnostic view is simply to read the published chart on the
indicator's [reference page](../reference/indicator-life-expectancy-bc.qmd),
which is regenerated from the same files on every render.

To make your own view, the two headline characteristics are:

- `Life expectancy (in years) at age x (ex)` with `age_group == "0 years"`
  — life expectancy at birth.
- `Number of deaths` and `Mortality rate per 1,000 population` in
  `data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv` — the mortality indicator.

Two habits the project expects of any view you build:

1. **Plot the whole window, not one point.** The trajectory JSON alongside
   each CSV states whether the series is stationary over its window and,
   if not, where the regimes break. Read the number *and* its window.
2. **Mark the regimes.** The COVID-19 period (2020–2024) is shaded on the
   published charts; regime breaks are drawn as dashed lines. A series
   that moves is not necessarily a series whose *rule* changed — the tests
   distinguish the two.

## 5. Read the caveats

Open the indicator's reference page and read its provenance table and
caveats. For life expectancy, the key caveat is that it is a **period**
measure — the average lifespan of a synthetic cohort under one year's
death rates [@statcan_life_table] — not anyone's expected lifespan and not
a statement about the health of the living.

## 6. Reflect

Note what the chart does *not* tell you. Life expectancy at birth says
nothing about morbidity, functional status, or wellbeing; a rising value
can coexist with worsening health among the living. This is exactly why
the project treats every indicator as a **proxy** for a domain, never the
state of health itself — the [explanation](../explanation/index.qmd)
section takes this up.

## What you have learned

The whole project follows the pattern you just walked: a catalogued
source → a fetch step → a reproducible build into tidy data with its
resolution recorded → a trajectory view that states its window and
regimes → a proxy that is read alongside its caveats. Every later
indicator and analysis reuses it.
